dataset.description: This dataset applies use state-of-the-art bias-adjustment methods developed for ISIMIP3b climate forcing and extends it to further CMIP6 models. The complete set of raw and bias-adjusted CMIP6 forcing data will be used in subsequent modelling activities (e.g., Tasks 2.2, 2.3, 3.2, 3.4, 4.1 and 5.4) and in the stakeholder co-design process (WP1). In stage 2, we will further develop and test the bias-adjustment methodology with a focus on extremes. New features for variability adjustment at different time scales will be added, and the resulting methodologies will be made available as open-source software. We will provide updated CMIP6 bias-adjusted data with the refined methodology of stage 2 (D2.1). Together with consortium partners, a selection of extreme events and biophysical impact categories that are particularly relevant for trade-offs and synergies between mitigation and adaptation strategies across Europe and the world will be made (MS7) to inform MESMER extensions and guide data extractions from the CMIP6 and ISIMIP archives. This will provide leading-edge hazard  information as input for Task 2.2 and WPs 3-5.

dataset.description:
Cluster dataset T3.1

The initial phase of this project involves conducting a cluster analysis on European regions at the NUTS-3 level to assess their socio-economic vulnerabilities to climate hazards and their adaptive capacity. The results of this analysis will be presented as a narrative within the JRC's Atlas of Demography, serving as a foundational exploration into subnational differentials in terms of climate vulnerability across Europe. This cluster analysis aims to provide valuable insights into variations at the subnational level, offering a comprehensive understanding of socio-economic vulnerability. The composite definition will encompass four primary components: 1) Demographic characteristics, such as age, sex, and educational attainment of the population. 2) Health indicators, elucidating the health status and potential morbidity at the subnational level. 3) Fertility dynamics, offering detailed insights into fertility differentials at the subnational level, thereby addressing infant and child exposure. 4) Economic factors, primarily involving GDP and poverty indicators, which play a pivotal role in adaptive capacity development in the event of hazard exposure.

Socioeconomic population projections at NUTS3 T3.1

As a subsequent phase in the cluster analysis, which is also designed to address collinearities and potential communal developments among diverse regions, the focus will shift towards generating a cohesive set of subnational population projections aligned with Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSP). These projections will encompass, at a minimum, age, sex, educational attainment, and urban/rural distribution for Europe at both the NUTS-2 and, when feasible, NUTS-3 levels. Emphasis will be placed on variables that have distinctly emerged as drivers of vulnerability and/or factors influencing adaptive capacities from the preceding analysis. This comprehensive set of projections aims to equip users with a powerful tool that, when intersected with future climate scenarios, will play a crucial role in identifying potential risk clusters at the European sub-national level. These findings are pivotal for the successful completion of other tasks and hold significant applications in formulating effective policies for exposure reduction and adaptation strategies to cope with changing climate conditions and extremes.

Vulnerability datasets – T3.2

Sub-national indicators of gender equality:
Increasing evidence on gender-differential vulnerability to climate change, including to climate hazards faced by European countries, suggests that risk assessments should adopt gender to represent an important layer of socio-economic determinants of climate impacts. For example, women tend to be disproportionally affected by heat stress, manifested both in increased mortality or dangers in pregnancy. The motivation behind developing this dataset is to provide a possibility to introduce gender-specific vulnerability in our risk assessments, on a sub-national spatial scale. To this end, new indicators of gender (in)equality (encompassing dimensions such as education, income, employment and/or health) will be developed and projected along the five scenarios of socioeconomic development over the 21st century. The spatial resolution of the data is planned to be at minimum on the NUTS-2 level, with a 5-year resolution. The historical data and the projections can be used in the portfolio of socio-economic indicators for assessments of vulnerability and adaptive capacity, in the context of climate risk assessment. They will also be used for a standalone analysis published as part of the Deliverable D.3.4.

dataset.description: MESMER is a spatially-resolved climate emulator. It replicates the behaviors of Earth system models, to emulate their variables at a lower computational cost. This model may be used to replicate the spatial & temporal evolutions for new scenarios, accounting for natural variability, thus of high interest for impact assessment. It is currently designed to emulate surface temperatures: annual mean (https://doi.org/10.5194/esd-11-139-2020), monthly mean (https://doi.org/10.5194/esd-13-851-2022) and annual maximum (https://doi.org/10.1029/2022GL099012); soil moistures (2 annual indicators at https://doi.org/10.5194/esd-14-1333-2023); fire weather (4 annual indicators at: https://doi.org/10.5194/esd-14-1333-2023). MESMER is developed on GitHub: https://github.com/MESMER-group/mesmer. Over the course of the project SPARCCLE, MESMER will be extended to other climate extreme and hazard indicators. It will be used to emulate such variables to emissions scenarios, such as newly developed climate mitigation/adaptation scenarios from WP5.

dataset.title: MESMER climate impact and extremes (WP2)

dataset.description:
CLIMADA is currently designed to model the probabilistic impacts of natural hazards (e.g., storms, heatwaves, wildfires, floods, ...) at any scale (building, city, regional, ..., global scales) and on any exposed element (buildings, people, crops, forests, ...). The model furthermore accounts for the vulnerability of the exposed elements. It can also incorporate changes in all components (e.g., climate change effects on hazards, socio-economic development or adaptation effects on exposures and vulnerability). The model can also account for any uncertainty distribution on the input variables, and derive the sensitivity of the output to these uncertainties. The final datasets produced are (probabilistic) impact matrices with one entry per exposure location per (probabilistic) hazard event. From these, various risk metrics such as return period curves or expected annual impacts can be produced. Furthermore, the cost and benefits of adaptation measures can be computed. CLIMADA is developed on GitHub: https://github.com/CLIMADA-project and has regular releases with associated DOI on Zenodo:  https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.8383171.
Based on the outputs from WP2 (for hazards), WP3 (for exposures and vulnerability) and WP5 (future pathways), risk distributions will be provided that can be integrated into CATSIM (T4.3) and IAMs (WP5, 6). In addition, data on the risk of natural hazards under climate change to certain global ecosystems will be provided.

format: CLIMADA uses open data formats for input data, and produced cliamte risk data can be exported to such formats. Most geo-data formats are usable, such as netcdf, geojson, gpk, geotiff, csv, excell, shape files. Internally, hdf5 file formats are used.

dmp.description:
The SPARCCLE project will produce a number of data sets for internal and public use. The list below provides an overview of the data sets to be generated within the project, along with the work packages that are responsible for these data sets (in parentheses):
  • CMIP6-ISIMIP forcing data (WP2)
  • MESMER climate impacts and extremes (WP2)
  • Granular socioeconomic projections incorporating gender and vulnerability (WP3)
  • Climate risk assessment (WP4)
  • Mitigation and adaptation pathways for Europe and the World  (WP5)
Care has been taken in the Data Management Plan to describe how the data will be FAIR—findable, accessible, interoperable and re-usable. The plan also describes the data that will be generated by the SPARCCLE project, whether and how they will be made accessible for verification and re-use, and how they will be curated and preserved.
The SPARCCLE Open Science Strategy (OSS, incorporating the open, living Data Management Plan) endeavours to use Open Science practices as a key mechanism to facilitate reporting and tracking of the project’s results and outcomes and maximize dissemination, exploitation and subsequent long-term impact. We will deliver this primarily through five ways, Open: software; datasets; publications; replicability scripts (e.g., that combine data and software to replicate results of a specific publication); and, integrated data exploration (SPARCCLE-Explorer and public API).
Where possible and strategic, this will be done using services from Open Access Infrastructure for Research in Europe (OpenAIRE), European Open Science Cloud and the Horizon Results Platform. We aim for a highly-connected network of research outputs, such that cross-referenced persistent identifiers exist between models, datasets, publications, replicability scripts and SPARCCLE-Explorer. SPARCCLE will ensure FAIR principles (findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable) for all datasets. SPARCCLE data will be findable through referencing with persistent Digital Object Identifiers (DOIs), and rich, standardized metadata, openly hosted in a trusted repository, like OpenAIRE or Zenodo, and tagged as a dataset community; accessible through the SPARCCLE-Explorer (Task 1.5), which will include open metadata provision, public API, and interactive visualizations for key variables; interoperable through the use of existing and established
data formats and conventions, such as NetCDF with CF conventions for spatial impacts and socioeconomics data or the standard .csv data template used by the IAMC since 2009 and IPCC WGIII since AR5; reusable through rich metadata as defined in the DMP, traceability through version control, permissive licensing (CC-BY or similar) and instructions on replicability. IIASA, PIK, ETHZ and CA ensure the long-term data availability beyond the project lifetime for at least 10 years. 
Each data set is described in detail further in the report, including information regarding standards and metadata, data sharing and archiving and preservation. The aim of the plan is to ensure that data produced by the project will satisfy the Horizon data management guidelines. The data plan will be updated periodically, and additional details for each data set will be added as the project advances.
To the degree it is compliant with data protection regulations, all research data sets produced in SPARCCLE are also intended to be used outside of the project. Experience in particular with existing scenario databases has shown that re-analysis and use of the data beyond the original purpose is pursued heavily if provided on-line (e.g., as in Horizon 2020 projects CD-LINKS and ENGAGE). The majority of scenario data for the SPARCCLE project will be hosted in a SPARCCLE Explorer and remain hosted there beyond the end of the project.
